name: Cavity prevention & decay
description: Understand what happens beneath the surface, and give your everyday routine a clear purpose.
keywords: The key takeaway  Early mineral loss can sometimes be reversed. An established cavity needs dental treatment.   What you can do today  Make your technique count:  see brushing and between-teeth guides .     01  How decay starts  Bacteria use sugars and starches to produce acids that remove minerals from enamel. Repeated exposure can lead to a cavity. Early decay may have no symptoms.    02  Early changes vs. a cavity  A white spot can signal early mineral loss. Saliva and fluoride can help repair enamel before a hole forms. Once a cavity develops, a dentist usually restores the damaged tooth with a filling.    03  Your everyday foundations  Brushing matters, but cavity risk also depends on frequent sugar exposure, saliva, fluoride, and other individual factors. Fluoride helps enamel resist mineral loss; sealants protect grooves on chewing surfaces. Brush with fluoride toothpaste, clean between teeth, and ask which additional prevention fits your risk.    04  When to book a visit  Pain or sensitivity deserves an assessment; it does not by itself confirm a cavity. Treatment depends on how much of the tooth is affected: a filling may repair a cavity, while deeper damage may require other treatment. For swelling, significant pain, or an injury, contact your dentist promptly.  Read the ADA emergency guide .

name: Get to know your gums
description: A simple guide to gum inflammation, periodontal disease, and the care that comes next.
keywords: The key takeaway  Bleeding gums deserve attention. A professional exam can tell you what is happening.   What you can do today  Notice changes in your gums? Book an assessment rather than trying to diagnose the stage yourself.     01  Notice the early signs  Swelling, tenderness, bleeding, persistent bad breath, or gums pulling away from teeth can signal a problem. Plaque can harden into tartar, which requires professional removal.    02  Gingivitis: inflammation at the gumline  Early gum disease can often improve with consistent brushing, cleaning between teeth, and professional care. Ask your dental team to demonstrate a technique that works for you.    03  Periodontitis: deeper support is affected  Periodontitis affects the tissues and bone that support teeth. Scaling and root planing, often called a deep cleaning, removes deposits below the gumline and cleans affected root surfaces. Some people need medication or surgery. Treatment and ongoing follow-up aim to control disease; home care remains important.    04  What your dental team checks  An examination may include gum-pocket measurements, your medical history, and X-rays to assess bone support. A single measurement alone is not a complete diagnosis. Loose teeth or pain when chewing should be assessed.

name: A healthier smile. A healthier you.
description: Oral health is part of whole-person care. Here is how to understand the connections without the alarm.
keywords: The key takeaway  A link between two conditions does not prove that one causes the other.   What you can do today  Update your medication list and share any health changes with your dental team.     01  What the research tells us  Researchers study links between gum disease and conditions including cardiovascular disease and pregnancy complications. Shared risk factors and inflammation may help explain these associations. Evidence of an association does not establish that dental treatment prevents those other conditions.    02  Diabetes and your mouth  Diabetes raises the likelihood of gum disease and may slow healing. Gum disease can also make blood sugar harder to manage. Share your diabetes history with your dental team and continue the care plan from your medical team.    03  Keep your care team connected  Bring an up-to-date medication list and tell your dental team about health changes, pregnancy, and ongoing treatment. Ask how these may affect your oral care.    04  Medications and dry mouth  Some medications can contribute to dry mouth, which raises the risk of decay and discomfort. Tell your dental and medical teams about persistent dryness, and discuss medication concerns with the prescriber before changing anything.  Compare dry mouth care formats .

name: More than a cleaning
description: Meet the prevention, assessment, and education behind a dental hygienist’s work.
keywords: The key takeaway  Your hygienist helps you understand your oral health and make a plan for everyday care.   What you can do today  Review your medication list before your next visit.     01  Assess and understand  Hygienists assess oral health, look for signs of disease, take dental X-rays, and share findings with the dentist. They document care so the team can follow changes over time.    02  Clean and protect  Removing plaque, tartar, and stains is part of preventive care. Hygienists may also apply fluoride or sealants to help protect teeth. Permitted services and supervision requirements vary by state and setting.    03  Make home care practical  Your hygienist focuses on prevention, assessment, and home-care education. The dentist diagnoses conditions and plans restorative treatment; their roles work together. Permitted responsibilities vary by state.    04  Make the most of your visit  A visit may include a health-history update, an examination, gum measurements, and cleaning. Your dentist decides whether X-rays are needed from your history and examination; they are not automatically needed at every visit. Share symptoms, medications, and anything that makes home care difficult. Ask when you should return based on your needs.
